title: The King of Kings Goes West: Naser al-Din Shah in Europe
subtitle: The Shah of Persia's first European tour and the hosts who watched him, April–September 1873
intro: In the spring of 1873 Naser al-Din Shah Qajar, who had ruled Persia for a quarter of a century, left Tehran for a journey no Persian monarch had made: five months by steamer, rail and carriage through Russia, Germany, Belgium, Britain, France, Switzerland, Italy, Austria and the Ottoman Empire, and home through the Caucasus. The trip was the project of his grand vizier, Mirza Hosein Khan Moshir od-Dowleh, who hoped that seeing Europe would win the Shah to railways, ministries and law, and that foreign courts would back the vast concession he had just granted to Baron Julius de Reuter.

The Shah kept a diary every day of the journey, and it was printed in Tehran on his return and translated into English by J. W. Redhouse in 1874. It is a plain, sometimes artless record of distances, meals, palaces, reviews, zoos and theatres, written by a king measuring other kings. It is also curious and frank: about Krupp's steam hammers and the soot of Manchester, the ruins of the Paris Commune, the poverty of southern Italy, and Russian improvements in a Tiflis that Persia had lost.

His hosts wrote back. In London, Queen Victoria's journal, the India Office minder Owen Tudor Burne, the Spectator and Punch, a visiting Mark Twain and a member of the Commons all set down what they saw of him, often on the same days he was writing about them. In Berlin an American diplomat sent home a sharp report on his manners. The record on this side is mostly newspapers, comic weeklies, despatches, parliamentary debate and a later memoir rather than private diaries, and it is labelled that way here.

Both sides' curiosity came mixed with condescension. London papers lectured each other on how to dazzle 'an Oriental', laughed at his table manners and later called his book schoolboyish; Punch made him a Persian cat. The Shah, for his part, read London crowds as personal devotion, judged peoples by their armies and their women, and wrote with the confidence of an absolute ruler. Behind the fireworks lay the Great Game: Britain courted Persia as a buffer against Russia, and Russia watched the courtship.

At home the tour had a cost. Clergy led by Mulla Ali Kani and a court faction around the Shah's wife Anis od-Dowleh, sent home from Moscow, turned against the minister and his concession. When the royal party landed back in Gilan in September, Mirza Hosein Khan was dismissed, and the Reuter concession was cancelled before the year was out. By then a Petersburg columnist could call the whole journey old news.
calendar_note: The Shah's diary is dated by the Islamic lunar (Hijri) calendar, year 1290 AH, and Redhouse prints the Christian (Gregorian) date beside each entry, e.g. 'Tuesday, 24th (22nd April)'. On the evidence of his headers, 1 Rabi' I 1290 fell on 29 April 1873, 1 Rabi' II on 28 May, 1 Jumada I on 27 June, and Jumada II began about 27 July; Rajab dates for late August and September are computed and marked c. Hijri months run 29 or 30 days, so a converted date can be a day off where the header is missing. Russian dates (Dostoevsky's Grazhdanin) are Old Style, twelve days behind the Gregorian calendar in 1873; date_iso always gives the Gregorian date. The Reuter concession of 25 July 1872 fell in Jumada I 1289.

eyes.name: Naser al-Din Shah Qajar
eyes.role: Shah of Persia since 1848, aged 41; the first Qajar ruler, and the first modern Persian monarch, to tour Europe
eyes.where: Tehran; then by Caspian, Volga and rail through Russia, Germany, Belgium, Britain, France, Switzerland, Italy, Austria, the Ottoman Empire and the Caucasus

waypoints.label: Vienna and the World's Fair, late July–Aug

eyes.authenticity: A daily journal kept (partly dictated) on the tour, first printed in instalments in the official Tehran gazette and as a court book, Ruznama-ye safar-e Farangestan (1874). The English version by J. W. Redhouse (John Murray, 1874) was commissioned by the British government and claims to be verbatim; a summarised version also appeared in 1874. The court edition was edited: less censored Persian texts published in the 1990s include personal remarks on royalty and women that the 1874 printing left out. A German 'translation' of 1874 was a fabrication by the novelist Michael Klapp.
eyes.bio: Naser al-Din had ruled for twenty-five years when his reforming chief minister persuaded him to see Europe for himself. He wrote in a plain, unadorned style that Redhouse compared to a private gentleman's, logging distances, meals, crowds, zoos, factories and theatres. His curiosity is real and his judgements are quick; he records Europe as a monarch measuring other monarchs and their machines, and as a traveller astonished by gas-light, railways and ironclads.

sources.title: Summarized translation with verbatim extracts, 1874 (Internet Archive)

eyes.name: Mirza Hosein Khan Moshir od-Dowleh (Sepahsalar)
eyes.role: Grand vizier (sadr-e a'zam) and commander-in-chief, aged about 45; former envoy at Constantinople; architect of the trip and of the Reuter concession
eyes.where: With the Shah throughout the tour; dismissed on landing back in Gilan
eyes.vantage_label: the minister who arranged the journey
eyes.form: official acts and correspondence (no diary); reported by others
eyes.authenticity: No diary. His role is documented through the concession he negotiated (25 July 1872), the British parliamentary record, and the Persian chronicles of his fall; his Persian correspondence survives in archives and later editions but is not used directly here.
eyes.bio: Mirza Hosein Khan had absorbed the Ottoman Tanzimat reforms during years at Constantinople and wanted Persia to borrow European railways, ministries and law. He brought the Shah to Europe to win him to that programme, and he negotiated the sweeping concession to Baron Reuter. Courtiers, a royal wife and senior clergy blamed him for both, and he fell the moment the royal party reached home.

eyes.name: Mulla Ali Kani
eyes.role: Leading mojtahed of Tehran, aged about 68
eyes.authenticity: His letter of protest to the Shah against the Reuter contract is cited in Persian scholarship and summarised in reference works; its exact date is not given in the sources consulted.
eyes.bio: Kani was the most powerful cleric in the capital. While the Shah toured Europe he wrote to demand that the Reuter contract be cancelled and its author dismissed, arguing that it handed a foreigner more than Britain had taken in India. His protest is the home front's answer to the ballrooms.

eyes.name: Queen Victoria
eyes.role: Queen of the United Kingdom, aged 54, still largely withdrawn from public life after Albert's death
eyes.authenticity: Her daily journal survives in Princess Beatrice's edited transcript (Royal Archives, online as Queen Victoria's Journals). Entries for 20 and 24 June 1873 are digested here from the published record of the visit; selections appear in the Letters of Queen Victoria, 2nd series (1926). No wording from the journal is quoted.
eyes.bio: Victoria disliked state visits and spent much of the Shah's stay out of London, but she received him at Windsor, invested him with the Garter and reviewed troops beside him. Her journal records a ruler she was obliged to court as a buffer against Russia, and a guest whose habits her household gossiped about.

sources.title: Royal Collection: Chevalier, Reception of the Shah at Windsor, 20 June 1873
Royal Collection: Chevalier, Review of troops, Windsor Great Park, 24 June 1873

eyes.name: Owen Tudor Burne
eyes.role: Major, India Office political secretary, aged 36; one of four British officials detailed to look after the Shah
eyes.where: Brussels, Dover, London, Windsor, Portsmouth, with the Shah
eyes.vantage_label: official minder at the visitor's elbow
eyes.authenticity: Major-General Sir Owen Tudor Burne, Memories (London: Edward Arnold, 1907), chapters IX–X, written from his notes and papers more than thirty years later; it reprints long extracts from the Shah's diary.
eyes.bio: Burne was asked by the Foreign Office on 4 June 1873 to help Sir Henry Rawlinson receive the Shah, and spent the visit in carriages, yachts and ballrooms with him. His memoir is a minder's view: fond, amused, sometimes condescending, and alert to the Great Game stakes behind the pageantry.

eyes.name: Samuel L. Clemens (Mark Twain)
eyes.role: American humorist, aged 37, in London as a special correspondent for the New York Herald
eyes.form: dated letters (newspaper correspondence and private letters)
eyes.authenticity: His 'Shah letters' to the New York Herald (summer 1873) and private letters of 18–19 June are calendared by the Mark Twain Project and the Twain's Geography day-by-day chronology.
eyes.bio: Twain crossed to Ostend to watch the Shah embark and came back on a British warship with the Shah's relatives and the press pack. His burlesque Herald letters ('bringing over the O'Shah') mock the frenzy of the London welcome as much as the visitor.

sources.title: Twain's Geography: England 1873 day by day

eyes.name: George Bancroft
eyes.role: United States Minister to the German Empire, aged 72, historian
eyes.vantage_label: foreign diplomat in the host capital
eyes.authenticity: Despatch to Secretary of State Hamilton Fish, Berlin, 16 June 1873, printed in Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1873.
eyes.bio: Bancroft watched the Berlin visit as an outsider to both monarchies and reported to Washington with republican dryness. His despatch is one of the bluntest host-side judgements of the Shah's manners.

eyes.name: The Spectator (London weekly)
eyes.role: Liberal weekly review, edited by R. H. Hutton and Meredith Townsend
eyes.authenticity: Unsigned leaders and news paragraphs, 1873–74, digitised in The Spectator Archive.
eyes.bio: Townsend, the paper's co-owner, had edited a newspaper in India and wrote on 'the East' with confident generalisation. The Spectator's columns show both the Russophobic strategy behind the welcome and the condescension with which London read its guest and, later, his book.

sources.title: Spectator, 7 June 1873, 'The Reception of the Shah'
Spectator, 28 June 1873, news of the week

eyes.name: Punch, or the London Charivari
eyes.role: Comic weekly; cartoons by John Tenniel and Linley Sambourne
eyes.vantage_label: the city laughing at the visit
eyes.authenticity: Punch vols 64–65 (June–July 1873), reproduced from HathiTrust scans on the Victorian Web.
eyes.bio: Punch turned the visit into a running joke for a month: Tenniel's British Lion courting a Persian cat, comic verse in the Shah's imagined voice, and the season's catchphrase 'Have you seen the Shah?' recycled for parliamentary cartoons. Its jokes cut both ways, at the guest and at London's craze for him.

sources.title: Victorian Web: Punch on the Shah's visit (index)

eyes.name: Alexander Baillie-Cochrane
eyes.role: Conservative MP for the Isle of Wight, aged 56
eyes.authenticity: Hansard, House of Commons, 23 July 1873, vol. 217, cc. 803–4.
eyes.bio: Baillie-Cochrane pressed the government on whether it had known of, or encouraged, the Reuter concession. His exchange with the Foreign Office shows how the Shah's visit and Persian railways became a Westminster question about Britain's rivalry with Russia.

eyes.name: Baron Paul Julius de Reuter
eyes.role: Founder of Reuters news agency, aged 56; concessionaire
eyes.form: other (concession text and letters, as reported in Parliament)
eyes.authenticity: The concession of 25 July 1872 and Reuter's letter to the Foreign Office of 12 September 1872 are summarised from the Foreign Office answer in Hansard, 23 July 1873.
eyes.bio: Reuter, a German-born naturalised Briton, obtained from the Shah a seventy-year monopoly on railways, mines, forests, irrigation and a customs farm. Curzon later called it the most complete surrender of a kingdom's resources ever dreamed of. The British government declined to back it, and it was cancelled within about a year.

eyes.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
eyes.role: Novelist, aged 51, editor of the conservative weekly Grazhdanin (The Citizen) in 1873
eyes.authenticity: Unsigned 'Foreign Events' columns in Grazhdanin, 1873, attributed to Dostoevsky by modern editors and printed on Russian Wikisource; dates are Old Style.
eyes.bio: Dostoevsky wrote the weekly foreign-affairs column while editing Grazhdanin. By autumn he could treat the Shah's journey, which had filled the European press all summer, as already old news, a sharp reminder of how quickly the spectacle faded.

entries.headline: A seventy-year concession for almost everything
entries.digest: The concession signed with the Shah's government grants Reuter a seventy-year monopoly on railways and tramways, mines other than precious metals, state forests, canals and irrigation, first refusal on a bank, and a 25-year customs farm. The Foreign Office later told Parliament that it first heard of the deal from a Tehran despatch received at the end of August.
entries.source_note: Hansard, Commons, 23 July 1873 (date of concession); Wikipedia, Reuter concession (terms)

entries.headline: The grand vizier signs Persia's railway future away
entries.digest: As grand vizier, Mirza Hosein Khan negotiates and backs the Reuter concession as the engine of his reform programme: foreign capital to build railways and ministries Persia cannot pay for itself. The same deal becomes the weapon his enemies will use against him a year later.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Mirza Hosein Khan Sepahsalar; Reuter concession

entries.headline: The Shah leaves his capital for Europe
entries.digest: The royal party leaves Tehran for the Caspian, with ministers, princes, servants and, at first, the favourite wife Anis od-Dowleh. Government at home is left to princes, with the Shah's son nominally in charge.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Diary of H.M. the Shah (start date 19 April); Redhouse diary opening chapter

entries.headline: Silk tents, horse races and a farewell audience
entries.digest: In the first camp outside the city he records horse races, a farewell audience for the foreign envoys, and the new silk tents pitched at Kan. The diary opens in the voice of a hunting monarch on a familiar road, not yet a traveller.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), opening entries (FB scan)

entries.headline: The Volga is like a sea
entries.digest: He lands at Astrakhan, which he calls by its old Persian-Turkic name, and marvels at the breadth of the Volga, the gateway to the empire that had taken Persia's Caucasian provinces fifty years before.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 1

entries.headline: Kremlin treasures and a ballet without words
entries.digest: In Moscow he tours the Kremlin armoury and crown jewels and the ethnographic museum, and is taken to a ballet, which he explains for Persian readers as a performance of dancing with no speech. Around Moscow, Anis od-Dowleh is sent back to Tehran because the veiling question cannot be squared with Russian court protocol.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 2; Wikipedia, Anis al-Dawla (sent home from Moscow)

entries.headline: Twenty thousand troops for the Shah
entries.digest: In St Petersburg Alexander II receives him warmly, gives him the Order of St Andrew in diamonds, and parades over twenty thousand troops on the Champ de Mars. He admires the Winter Palace and Hermitage and attends a nobles' ball, and describes the Emperor as grave in speech.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 2 (entries 23–26 May)

entries.headline: Berlin, and an emperor of seventy-six
entries.digest: After a fast run across East Prussia he reaches Berlin, where the aged Wilhelm I personally shows him his apartments. He notes the Emperor's age with something like admiration.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 3

entries.headline: Dinner with Bismarck, Roon and Moltke
entries.digest: After the zoo and aquarium he dines with the Emperor among the men who had just beaten France: Bismarck, Roon and Moltke. The next day eighteen thousand troops march past, and he sums up the kingdom as a state made of soldiers.
entries.quote: The Prussian kingdom is all soldiery
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 3 (3–4 June)

entries.headline: The Foreign Office drafts a minder
entries.digest: Burne is asked to help Sir Henry Rawlinson receive the Shah and becomes one of four officials, with Sir Arnold Kemball and Captain Grey, responsible for the visitor's comfort and programme.
entries.source_note: Burne, Memories (1907), ch. IX

entries.headline: Krupp's hammers, like mountains
entries.digest: At Krupp's works at Essen he watches steam hammers forging guns and describes the plant as a mighty city of furnaces, then goes on to Cologne's gardens and Rhine bridge.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 3 (phrase from OCR extract)

entries.headline: How to impress an 'Oriental': the Spectator's advice
entries.digest: Before the visit the Spectator argues that the Shah will judge by sheer mass, so a modest review will not impress him and British ironclads cannot reach the Caspian anyway. It urges a ride through the crowds or an 'Arabian Nights' night at the Crystal Palace, frets about Persia as Russia's road to India, and doubts he will learn anything from parliaments.
entries.quote: An Oriental judges everything by mass
entries.source_note: Spectator, 7 June 1873, p. 8

entries.headline: An American minister unimpressed
entries.digest: Bancroft reports to Washington that the Shah made a poor impression on Germans: apathetic, keeping a Potsdam court waiting over an hour, eating strawberries straight from the serving dish with a fork. He compares him to a spoiled child.
entries.quote: rather the air of a semi-civilized chieftain
entries.source_note: FRUS 1873, doc. 142, Bancroft to Fish, 16 June 1873

entries.headline: The minders meet their charge
entries.digest: Burne and his colleagues, barred by etiquette from joining the suite on Belgian soil, are received at Brussels, where the Shah is reported unwell. Burne thinks he does not look at all well.
entries.source_note: Burne, Memories (1907), ch. IX

entries.headline: Twain crosses to watch the Shah embark
entries.digest: Clemens and his secretary cross to Ostend to cover the Shah's arrival on the coast, and stay overnight among the correspondents waiting for the royal train from Brussels.
entries.source_note: Twain's Geography, England 1873 day by day, 17 June

entries.headline: A calm Channel and English princes at Dover
entries.digest: He crosses from Ostend in fine weather, is met at Dover by English princes and officials, and goes by train to London to be lodged in Buckingham Palace.
entries.quote: like the palm of one's hand
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 4 (simile for the calm sea, from OCR extract)

entries.place: HMS Vigilant, Ostend to Dover; London
entries.headline: Manned yards, cheering steamers, rain at the palace
entries.digest: Aboard the Vigilant, Burne watches the Channel Fleet salute with manned yards and Dover excursion steamers cheer. The Shah assumes the crowds were sent by the government; the Buckingham Palace arrival is spoiled by a shower.
entries.source_note: Burne, Memories (1907), ch. IX

entries.headline: Back with the press pack, writing the first Shah letter
entries.digest: Clemens returns on HMS Lively with members of the Shah's family and the journalists, and that day writes his first Herald letter on the visit, 'The Man of Mark Ready to Bring Over the O'Shah'. He also asks his American publisher to rush the pieces out uncopyrighted as a cheap pamphlet.
entries.source_note: Twain's Geography, 18 June 1873

entries.headline: The Queen invests him with the Garter
entries.digest: At Windsor the Queen receives him and with her own hand invests him with the Order of the Garter; he finds her cheerful and pleasant. That evening he attends the City's entertainment given by the Lord Mayor.
entries.quote: She is very cheerful and pleasant of countenance.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 4 (quote as given in OCR extract)

entries.headline: Receiving the Shah at the Sovereign's Entrance
entries.digest: The Queen meets the Shah at the Sovereign's Entrance with her younger children around her, takes him through the castle, and invests him with the Garter while he confers the Persian Order of the Lion and Sun on her. Her journal records the ceremony and her impressions of a guest Britain needed as a friend against Russia.
entries.source_note: Chevalier watercolour, RCIN 920788 (scene); Burne, Memories ch. IX (exchange of orders); journal wording not consulted

entries.headline: Garter at Windsor, freedom of the City at night
entries.digest: Burne records the exchange of orders at Windsor and the Guildhall ball, where the Lord Mayor presents an address and the freedom of the City.
entries.source_note: Burne, Memories (1907), ch. IX

entries.headline: Tenniel's 'Feline Friends'
entries.digest: Punch's double-page cartoon by John Tenniel shows the British Lion making up to a Persian 'chat', the pun casting the Shah's visit as a courtship between two cats over the road to India.
entries.source_note: Punch 64 (21 June 1873), 256–57, via Victorian Web

entries.headline: A day of rest among hippos and sea lions
entries.digest: He spends his Sunday at the Zoo, describing the hippopotamuses, a performing monkey and sea lions, and the crowds that press round him, which he reads as affection for his person.
entries.quote: they do entertain a love towards us
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 4; Burne, Memories ch. IX (Zoo chosen for day of rest)

entries.headline: Through a street of men-of-war
entries.digest: He steams down lines of warships that fire salutes, goes aboard the ironclads Agincourt and Sultan, and nearly has his boat struck by a steamer's paddle-wheel. In the evening there is a concert at the Albert Hall.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 4

entries.headline: The royal yacht nearly capsizes
entries.digest: Burne remembers the naval review for a near-disaster when a paddle-wheel blunder almost upset the royal party's vessel, and the Albert Hall that night packed with some fourteen thousand people.
entries.source_note: Burne, Memories (1907), ch. IX

entries.headline: Troops before the Queen, a sabre for the Duke
entries.digest: At Windsor he watches troop manoeuvres beside the Queen and presents a jewelled sabre to the Duke of Cambridge. A dinner at Lord Granville's becomes a ball at the Foreign Office.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 4

entries.headline: Side by side at the saluting point
entries.digest: The Queen takes the salute of the Household and other troops with the Shah beside her, both royal standards flying; she later has the scene painted for her collection.
entries.source_note: Chevalier watercolour, RCIN 913315 (scene and provenance); Spectator, 28 June 1873

entries.headline: The merchant river: the best lesson of the visit
entries.digest: A river trip past the docks to Goschen's luncheon at Greenwich is, for Burne, the most instructive sight of the whole visit: ships of every trade, not just warships, crowding to salute.
entries.source_note: Burne, Memories (1907), ch. IX

entries.headline: Locomotives at Crewe, a city black with soot
entries.digest: He sees locomotives built at Crewe and a Manchester mill with some two thousand looms, and notes that the city's walls, windows, people and even clothes are blackened by smoke, so that the ladies wear black.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 4; Burne, Memories ch. X (extract)

entries.headline: A hard-worked guest, and a fleet that failed to awe
entries.digest: The Spectator's week in review describes a Shah 'very hardly worked', a magnificent Guildhall evening marred by etiquette slips, and a Greenwich river day that it thinks impressed him more than Spithead. A second paragraph praises the Windsor review but calls the railway arrangements execrable.
entries.source_note: Spectator, 28 June 1873, p. 1–2

entries.headline: Lord Russell explains Whigs and Tories
entries.digest: Rain spoils sightseeing at Kew, so he calls on the elderly former prime minister Lord Russell, who explains the two parties to him, and takes tea at Richmond.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 4 (date header unclear in OCR)

entries.headline: Fireworks, and a jeer for the Tsarevich
entries.digest: At the Crystal Palace fête, Burne notes, the crowd cheers the Shah but greets the visiting Russian heir with hostile cries, a flash of the Russophobia beneath the welcome. A fire-brigade display and an arranged boxing match also belong to these days.
entries.source_note: Burne, Memories (1907), chs IX–X

entries.headline: The best pleasure ground in London
entries.digest: He tours the glass palace and its gardens, watches acrobats and the great fountains, and stays for fireworks, ranking it the finest place of amusement in London; he asks to go back a second time.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 4; two visits noted in Evening Star (NZ), 4 Sept 1873, via Papers Past

entries.headline: Leaving England under an escort of ironclads
entries.digest: Crowds see him off from Victoria; after a rough rail journey he boards a French vessel at Portsmouth, escorted out by British warships and met by French ones off Cherbourg at sunset. Nearly everyone aboard falls sick.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 5

entries.headline: MacMahon at Passy, and the ruins of the Commune
entries.digest: He reaches Paris, greeted by Marshal MacMahon (who had replaced Thiers in May) and the Duc de Broglie. He records the Tuileries, the Hôtel de Ville and the Vendôme column wrecked two years earlier in the Commune, and a French people still in mourning after defeat.
entries.quote: is now a mass of ruins
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 5; Tehran Bureau, 'How Paris bedazzled a Persian king'

entries.headline: 'The Shah's Impressions': Punch puts words in his mouth
entries.digest: A comic poem has the Shah conclude that London's bowing crowds prove him king of kings, and that the Prussian state is ruled by the stick, mocking both the visitor's vanity and the hosts' grovelling.
entries.quote: I am King of Kings and Lord of Lords!
entries.source_note: Punch 65 (12 July 1873), 11, via Victorian Web

entries.headline: Seven hundred deputies and eighty thousand troops
entries.digest: At Versailles he watches the National Assembly sitting with some seven hundred members and a speaker too quiet to be heard; at Longchamp he reviews about eighty thousand troops and notes the elegant women among the spectators.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 5 (undated entries)

entries.headline: 'Have you seen the Shah?' becomes a political joke
entries.digest: Sambourne's Essence of Parliament cartoon shows Disraeli turning a dazzling mirror on Gladstone, captioned with the summer's catchphrase about the Shah. A month after his arrival the visit has become shorthand for any blinding show.
entries.source_note: Punch 65 (19 July 1873), 2, via Victorian Web

entries.headline: Is the Reuter concession 'extraordinary' and 'dangerous'?
entries.digest: Baillie-Cochrane asks whether the government knew of the Reuter negotiations and will publish the Tehran correspondence. The Speaker strikes 'extraordinary' and 'dangerous' from his question; Lord Enfield replies that the Foreign Office learned of the concession only after it was signed.
entries.source_note: Hansard, Commons, 23 July 1873, vol. 217 cc. 803–4

entries.headline: A king who did not eat
entries.digest: Victor Emmanuel II shows him the royal armoury and gives a dinner at which, he notes, the king himself eats nothing, then presents mosaics and portraits.
entries.quote: The Sovereign himself partook of no food.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 6

entries.headline: Persia's thin showing at the World's Fair
entries.digest: The Emperor guides him through the national courts of the Exhibition. He admits the Persian section is thin because the order to send goods went out late, though he praises its fine fabrics and wares.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 6 (undated Exhibition entry)

entries.headline: Olive groves and poor people
entries.digest: He boards an Ottoman ship at Brindisi and remarks on the olive groves and the poverty of the people of southern Italy, a rare note on European want.
entries.quote: The people of these parts are extremely poor.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 6

entries.headline: Into the Sultan's capital
entries.digest: Met at the Dardanelles by the grand vizier on the Sultan's behalf, he transfers to an Ottoman vessel for the Bosphorus, while Persian subjects of the city come out by steamer to greet him.
entries.source_note: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), chapter 7

entries.headline: A town transformed under Russian rule
entries.digest: Arriving by train at Tiflis, he recalls it as wretched and filthy fifty years earlier and notes its new houses, schools and paved streets, as well as its mixed population and its fruit, an uncomfortable compliment to the empire that had taken it from Persia.
entries.source_note: RFE/RL article quoting the diary (Caucasus section)

entries.headline: A mojtahed's letter: cancel the contract, dismiss the minister
entries.digest: Kani writes to the Shah that the Reuter contract gives a foreigner more than Britain gained in India, that the clergy are duty-bound to speak against misgovernment, and that the deal must be cancelled and the minister behind it dismissed.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Mulla Ali Kani (letter undated)

entries.headline: Home across the Caspian
entries.digest: After a dry, cheerless road from Tiflis by Ganja to Baku, which he calls a wretched lodging, he crosses the Caspian and lands at Enzeli, ending the European tour.
entries.source_note: Burne, Memories (reached Persia 7 Sept); Wikipedia, Diary of H.M. the Shah

entries.headline: Dismissed on Persian soil
entries.digest: Within days of landing, under pressure from princes, courtiers gathered round Anis od-Dowleh and the Tehran clergy, the Shah removes him as grand vizier and leaves him behind as governor of Gilan. Accounts differ on the details, including a brief reinstatement on the road.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Anis al-Dawla; Mirza Hosein Khan Sepahsalar

entries.headline: Already forgotten: the Shah's journey
entries.digest: In his foreign-affairs column, Dostoevsky observes that the news of the season has buried everything before it: the Vienna Exhibition and the Shah's journey now feel like events from long ago.
entries.source_note: Grazhdanin, 'Inostrannye sobytiya', 17 Sept 1873, Russian Wikisource

entries.headline: Back as foreign minister
entries.digest: Weeks after his fall and the concession's cancellation, he returns to government as minister of foreign affairs, a post he holds until 1880.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Mirza Hosein Khan Sepahsalar (infobox)

entries.headline: Reviewing the Shah's diary: 'a Court Journal'
entries.digest: Reviewing Redhouse's translation, the Spectator finds the diary boyish and simple, valuable only for its truthfulness, a royal court circular full of meals, near-accidents and crowd counts. It allows that such simplicity can coexist with real capacity to rule, then closes with a jibe that the East never changes.
entries.quote: It is a Court Journal he has written
entries.source_note: Spectator, 10 Oct 1874, p. 10

claims.claim: Explains the ballet for Persians as dancing and acting without words
claims.evidence: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), Moscow entries

claims.claim: Sums up Prussia as a kingdom made entirely of soldiers
claims.evidence: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), Berlin review

claims.claim: Claims that 'an Oriental' judges only by mass and must be dazzled, not instructed
Calls the Shah apathetic, ill-mannered at table and like a spoiled child
Notes the Shah believed the cheering Dover crowds were sent by the government
Finds Queen Victoria cheerful and pleasant, and records her investing him herself
claims.evidence: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), Windsor entry

claims.claim: Draws the visit as the British Lion courting a Persian cat over the road to India
Reads London's curious crowds as personal love for the Shah
claims.evidence: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), Zoo entry

claims.claim: Judges the merchant Thames the most instructive sight of the visit
Describes Manchester as so sooty that buildings, people and clothes are all black
claims.evidence: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), Manchester entry

claims.claim: Suspects the Shah was more struck by merchant ships than by the war fleet
Sees Paris in ruins after the Commune and the French sunk in mourning
claims.evidence: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), Paris entries

claims.claim: Imagines the Shah taking all the bowing as proof he is king of kings
Remarks on the poverty of the people of southern Italy
claims.evidence: Redhouse tr., The Diary of H.M. the Shah of Persia (Murray, 1874), Brindisi entry

claims.claim: Admits Tiflis has been rebuilt and cleaned under Russian rule
Dismisses the diary as a schoolboyish court journal and the East as unchanging

convergences.label: London prepares its welcome (4–21 June)
convergences.note: The India Office drafts minders, the Spectator lectures on how to dazzle 'an Oriental', and Punch's Lion courts a Persian cat: three versions of the same Great Game calculation, from the official, the editorial and the comic angle.

convergences.label: The Berlin week (31 May – 6 June)
convergences.note: The Shah dines with Bismarck and Moltke and admires a kingdom of soldiers; the American minister, watching the same week, sees only bad table manners and a court kept waiting.

convergences.label: Ostend to Dover
convergences.note: The Shah notes a calm sea and royal princes; Burne the manned yards and cheering steamers, and the Shah's belief that the cheers were organised; Twain rides back with the press pack and turns it all into burlesque by nightfall.

convergences.label: Windsor and the Garter
convergences.note: Each side records the exchange of orders: the Garter for the Shah, the Lion and Sun for the Queen. He writes of her kindness; her journal and her commissioned painting fix the scene as a diplomatic necessity.

convergences.label: The naval review at Spithead
convergences.note: Both the Shah and Burne remember the near-collision with a paddle-wheel more than the fleet; the Spectator suspects the warships, which could never reach the Caspian, impressed him less than the merchant Thames.

convergences.label: Review in Windsor Great Park
convergences.note: Sovereign and guest take the salute together; the Shah records the jewelled sabre he gives away, the press records two hours lost on the Great Western.

convergences.label: The Crystal Palace fête
convergences.note: The Shah ranks it the best pleasure ground in London; Burne hears the same crowd jeer the Russian heir, the rivalry behind the fireworks.

convergences.label: The Reuter concession reaches Westminster
convergences.note: While the Shah is in Paris and Geneva, the Commons debates the deal his grand vizier signed and Reuter promoted; the government distances itself, a signal that will help sink both concession and minister.

convergences.label: Homecoming and the fall of the reformer
convergences.note: The Shah lands at Enzeli and writes up his return; the clergy's letter and the court faction bring down his minister; in Petersburg a columnist already files the whole journey under old news.

ties.note: Received at Windsor on 20 June and side by side at the Windsor review on 24 June; they exchanged the Garter and the Lion and Sun.
Burne was one of four British officials attached to the Shah for the whole English visit, and later reprinted long extracts of his diary.
The grand vizier who planned the journey and travelled with the Shah; dismissed by him on their return.
Negotiating partners in the concession of 25 July 1872.
Kani demanded the minister's dismissal and the cancellation of his contract with Reuter.
Baillie-Cochrane's Commons question of 23 July 1873 was entirely about Reuter's concession.
Twain followed the Shah from Ostend and wrote a series of burlesque Herald letters about him.
Bancroft's despatch of 16 June 1873 is a report on the Shah's behaviour in Berlin and Potsdam.
The Spectator wrote about the Shah throughout the visit and reviewed his diary in English translation in October 1874.
Both London weeklies traded on the same summer craze, one with leaders on Persia and Russia, the other with cartoons and verse.
Two comic treatments of the same London welcome, written within days of each other.
Dostoevsky's Grazhdanin column of September 1873 names the Shah's journey as a faded news story.

threads_out.note: The Iwakura embassy from Japan was touring the same courts and factories in 1872–73 and visited the Vienna World's Fair in June 1873, weeks before the Shah: two Asian governments studying Europe in the same season.
Four years later Guo Songtao, China's first resident minister in London, recorded the same institutions (Parliament, Woolwich, the Crystal Palace) that the Shah toured in 1873.
Naser al-Din made a third European tour in 1889 and visited the Paris Exposition Universelle, the event of that chapter; he kept a diary of that journey too.
The Indo-European Telegraph line, completed through Persia in 1870, carried news of the tour; Reuter's agency, which lived on such cables, was the source of the concession that shadowed the visit.
